title: Vibrating Air
question: What must a surface do in order to produce a sound?
correctExplanation: Right. A moving surface repeatedly disturbs the air, and those pulses travel to the ear.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is vibrations. Energy from a moving object disturbs the surrounding air and travels as a wave.
lessonContent:
Moving parts push the air around them.
Rapid back-and-forth motion reaches the ear.
Stillness makes no sound at all.
Motion is the source of every tone.
Share this: feel one speaker tonight and describe what it is doing.

title: Silent Void
question: Through which of these can sound not travel at all?
correctExplanation: Right. With no particles to pass the motion along, a wave has nothing to carry it.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a vacuum. With no particles to collide, the wave has no medium to travel through.
lessonContent:
Sound needs matter to carry it.
Empty space offers nothing to pass motion along.
Astronauts cannot hear each other outside.
Every wave needs a medium.
Share this: explain tonight why space is silent.

title: Repeating Rate
question: The number of times a sound wave repeats each second is called what?
correctExplanation: Right. The repeat rate, counted in cycles per second, is the key property of a tone.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is its frequency. The repeat rate, measured in hertz, determines how high the note sounds.
lessonContent:
The repeat rate sets how high a note sounds.
Measure it in cycles per second.
Doubling the rate raises the note.
Rate and spacing trade off.
Share this: compare two tones tonight and guess which repeats faster.

title: High or Low
question: How high or low a note seems to a listener is called what?
correctExplanation: Right. The ear reads the repeat rate as height, and musicians name notes accordingly.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is pitch. It rises with the rate of repetition and falls as the rate drops.
lessonContent:
The ear reads repeat rate as height.
Faster repetition sounds higher.
Slower repetition sounds lower.
Musicians name this property with letters.
Share this: hum a low note and a high note and notice the difference.

title: Size of the Swing
question: How loud a sound is depends mainly on the size of its what?
correctExplanation: Right. Larger swings carry more energy, which the ear reads as volume.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is amplitude. The size of each swing determines how loud the sound feels.
lessonContent:
Bigger swings carry more energy.
The size of each swing sets the volume.
Gentle motion makes a faint sound.
Strong motion makes a loud one.
Share this: tap a table softly then firmly and compare.

title: Loudness Scale
question: Which unit is used to measure how loud a sound is?
correctExplanation: Right. Loudness uses a compressed, logarithmic scale rather than a simple count.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the decibel. Loudness uses a logarithmic scale where each step multiplies the energy.
lessonContent:
Loudness is measured on a compressed scale.
The scale is logarithmic, not linear.
Quiet rooms sit near the bottom.
Concerts push toward the top.
Share this: check the volume reading on one device tonight.

title: Sound Reflections
question: What do you call a sound that returns to you after bouncing off a distant wall?
correctExplanation: Right. A hard, distant surface can throw sound back with a noticeable delay.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is an echo. The reflected sound arrives late enough to be heard separately.
lessonContent:
Hard surfaces send sound back.
The return arrives after a short delay.
Large empty halls make the effect obvious.
Soft furnishings absorb the return.
Share this: clap in a large empty room tonight and listen.

title: Speed of Sound
question: About how fast does sound travel through ordinary air?
correctExplanation: Right. That works out to roughly a third of a kilometre each second.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is about 340 metres per second. It is far slower than light, which is why you see lightning before thunder.
lessonContent:
Sound moves far slower than light.
That delay explains distant flashes and late thunder.
Roughly a third of a kilometre each second.
Count the gap to estimate distance.
Share this: time the gap between lightning and thunder tonight.

title: Above Hearing
question: What is sound with a repeat rate too high for the human ear to detect called?
correctExplanation: Right. Some animals and medical devices use tones beyond our upper limit.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is ultrasound. Its rate is too high for the human ear but useful in medicine and animal navigation.
lessonContent:
The ear has upper limits.
Some animals hear beyond ours.
Medical devices use these high tones.
Bats navigate with them.
Share this: look up one animal that hears what humans cannot.

title: Natural Rhythm
question: A swing pushed at its natural rhythm rises higher each time. What is this effect called?
correctExplanation: Right. Matching the object's favoured rhythm adds energy with every cycle.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is resonance. Pushing at the natural rhythm adds energy with every cycle.
lessonContent:
Every object has a favoured rhythm.
Matching that rhythm adds energy each cycle.
Small pushes accumulate into large swings.
Bridges and glasses can be affected too.
Share this: notice one object that reacts strongly to a particular rhythm.

title: Passing Siren
question: A siren seems higher as it approaches and lower as it recedes. What is this called?
correctExplanation: Right. Motion bunches the waves ahead of the source and stretches those behind.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the Doppler effect. Motion compresses waves ahead of a source and stretches them behind.
lessonContent:
Motion changes the spacing of waves.
Approaching sources bunch their waves.
Receding sources stretch them.
The same happens with light from distant stars.
Share this: listen to a passing vehicle tonight and track the change.

title: Doubling Rate
question: A note with double the repeat rate of another is one what higher?
correctExplanation: Right. Doubling the rate sounds like the same lettered note one interval higher.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is an octave. Doubling the rate produces the same lettered note one interval higher.
lessonContent:
Musical notes relate by simple ratios.
Doubling the rate sounds like the same note higher.
That interval gets its own name.
The scale repeats every doubling.
Share this: sing a note then its doubled version.

title: Violin or Flute
question: A violin and a flute play the same note, yet they sound different. What quality differs?
correctExplanation: Right. Each instrument mixes overtones differently, giving a note its distinctive voice.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is timbre. The mix of overtones gives each instrument its distinctive voice.
lessonContent:
Instruments mix many tones at once.
The blend of overtones differs by instrument.
That is why a note can have a voice.
Two sources at the same height still differ.
Share this: identify one instrument by sound alone tonight.

title: Pulsing Tones
question: Two nearly equal tones played together produce a slow pulsing. What is it called?
correctExplanation: Right. Slightly different rates drift in and out of step, creating a slow throb.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is beats. Slightly different rates drift in and out of phase, creating a slow pulse.
lessonContent:
Slightly mismatched rates drift in and out.
The waves reinforce then cancel.
You hear a slow throb.
Tuning instruments relies on this.
Share this: compare two nearly matched tones and listen for the throb.

title: Hearing Range
question: What is the approximate range of normal human hearing?
correctExplanation: Right. Young ears catch a wide band, though the upper end fades with age.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 20 hertz to 20000 hertz. The upper limit drops with age and noise damage.
lessonContent:
Young ears catch a wide band of rates.
The lower end extends far down.
The upper end fades with age.
Noise exposure narrows it faster.
Share this: test the highest tone you can still hear.

title: First to Shake
question: Which part of the ear is the first to move when sound arrives?
correctExplanation: Right. A thin membrane seals the canal and passes incoming motion to the bones behind.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the eardrum. It seals the canal and passes incoming motion to the small bones behind it.
lessonContent:
A thin membrane stretches across the canal.
Air pulses make it move.
Small bones then pass the motion inward.
It seals the inner chamber.
Share this: learn the name of one part of the ear tonight.

title: Steady Reference
question: Which small metal tool rings at a fixed note when struck?
correctExplanation: Right. Its shape fixes a single steady note that barely drifts.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a tuning fork. Its fixed shape gives a steady reference note for tuning.
lessonContent:
A metal bar with two prongs rings cleanly.
Its shape fixes a single steady note.
Musicians use it to set their pitch.
The note barely changes over time.
Share this: compare two voices to a steady reference note.

title: Faster Than Sound
question: What is the loud crack called when an aircraft outruns the speed of sound?
correctExplanation: Right. Waves pile up and release together when an object passes its own sound.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a sonic boom. Waves bunch up ahead of an object that outruns its own sound and release in one crack.
lessonContent:
Waves pile up when a source outruns them.
They release together in a sudden crack.
The object has passed its own sound.
People on the ground hear one loud report.
Share this: look up the speed of sound in your units tonight.

title: Dense Medium
question: Through which state of matter does sound travel fastest?
correctExplanation: Right. Tightly packed, elastic particles pass the motion along most quickly.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a solid. Closely packed, elastic particles transmit the wave faster than liquids or gases.
lessonContent:
Tightly packed particles pass motion quickly.
Loose gases slow the wave down.
Dense elastic materials carry it best.
Railway tracks transmit it far.
Share this: tap a table and listen for sound through the material.

title: Rate and Spacing
question: How are a sound wave's repeat rate and its spacing related?
correctExplanation: Right. Higher rates compress the spacing, and lower rates stretch it out.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is they are inversely related. As the rate rises, the spacing between cycles shrinks, keeping their product constant.
lessonContent:
Higher rates compress the spacing.
Lower rates stretch it out.
The product of the two stays constant.
That constant is the speed of sound.
Share this: reason about spacing for one tone tonight.

title: Rising Rate
question: If a tone's repeat rate increases, what happens to how high it sounds?
correctExplanation: Right. Height tracks repetition, so more cycles each second means a higher note.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it rises. A faster repeat rate always sounds higher to the ear.
lessonContent:
Height tracks the rate of repetition.
More cycles each second means a higher note.
Fewer cycles means a lower note.
Changing the rate changes the note.
Share this: slide a tuning control and describe the change in height.

title: Hall Design
question: A concert hall's shape and panels mainly control what?
correctExplanation: Right. Designers steer the bounces so every seat hears the performance clearly.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is reflections of sound. Designers shape how sound bounces so every seat hears clearly.
lessonContent:
Sound bounces off every hard surface.
Designers steer those bounces.
Panels and curves shape what the audience hears.
Too much bounce muddles the music.
Share this: listen for the room in a recording tonight.

title: Cancelling Waves
question: How do noise-cancelling headphones reduce outside sound?
correctExplanation: Right. An opposite wave meets the incoming one and cancels it where they overlap.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is they add a mirror wave. An opposite wave cancels the incoming one where they overlap.
lessonContent:
A microphone samples the incoming noise.
Electronics create an opposite wave.
The two waves cancel where they meet.
The result is near silence.
Share this: notice one technology that works by cancellation.

title: Travelling Squeeze
question: Sound is a travelling wave of changing what?
correctExplanation: Right. Air bunches and spreads, and that push travels outward from the source.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is pressure. Sound is a travelling change in the push of the air.
lessonContent:
Air molecules bunch and spread.
That push travels outward from a source.
Your ear reads the passing squeeze.
Every sound is a travelling disturbance.
Share this: feel the air from a speaker tonight.

title: Lowest Mode
question: What is the lowest repeat rate of a vibrating string called?
correctExplanation: Right. It is the simplest pattern of motion, with higher ones layered above it.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the fundamental. It is the lowest pattern of motion, with higher ones layered above it.
lessonContent:
A string can move in many patterns.
The simplest pattern has the lowest rate.
Higher patterns layer on top of it.
Together they shape the instrument's voice.
Share this: pluck a string and listen for the lowest steady tone.
